summary:
Puno is a department of Peru, and every legal measure bearing on trans visitors there is national in scope. The sources record no Puno-specific application, exemption, local ordinance or documented enforcement practice; what follows is the Peruvian framework as it binds the department.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code, which replaced an 1863 code that had criminalised sodomy at penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity. Its underlying bills 6506 and 8457/2023-CR were presented by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia. The Women and Family Commission approved a merged draft unanimously on 20 February 2025, barring entry to restrooms that do not correspond to birth sex while allowing exceptions for custody situations, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and banning so-called ambiguous bathroom signage. The bill's stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their biological sex, subject to narrow listed exceptions. A legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the IDEHPUCP human-rights institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, dated 15 April 2025, holds that the provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory and warned that restroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. IDEHPUCP finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks, and invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by biological sex, which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed transsexualism a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to gender discordance in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on public order and security grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to go use the men's room.
tangentialFactors:
Peru is one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, that offer no anti-discrimination coverage on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds, a regional standing that shapes how far a visitor can rely on formal complaint mechanisms.

The restroom restriction's origins lie in a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport, and Gianna Camacho's objection that enforcement would turn on security staff discretion, including identity-document checks, identifies transit and screening points as the places where a trans visitor is most likely to be challenged.

The 1863 Penal Code criminalised sodomy at penalties comparable to rape before the 1924 code decriminalised it, a historical backdrop to the current absence of statutory bias-motivation provisions in the Penal Code.

No source in the inventory reports any incident, arrest, prosecution or complaint arising under Law 32331 or the April 2025 sexual-integrity law in Puno, so the department's practical risk profile is inferred from national law alone.
